d.title: The proxy keeps climbing while true quality collapses
d.caption: The reward model is a **proxy** fitted from finite comparisons, and its direction is only **0.5931 cosine — 53.6 degrees — from the true one**. Optimise the proxy and you move partly toward quality and partly sideways. The table is the consequence: the proxy score rises linearly forever while the true score peaks around KL 1.0 and then falls, reaching **−9.0413 at KL 6.0 while the proxy reads 6.0000**. Anyone watching the training reward sees a successful run throughout.

d.title: A better reward model buys headroom, in closed form
d.caption: If true quality is c·s − 0.35s² where c is the cosine alignment and s the distance moved, the peak is at **s∗ = c/0.70** — a closed form, so unlike the cosines themselves it is not subject to sampling noise. Fitting the reward model on more pairs raises c and therefore pushes the peak further out: from **0.4799 at 50 pairs to 0.9980 at 100,000**, moving the best achievable true score from 0.1645 to **0.7115**. So more preference data does not just make the proxy better — it extends how hard you are allowed to optimise.

d.title: A held-out gold reward model is the cheapest warning available
d.caption: The training reward is useless as a signal — it rises monotonically through the collapse. A **second reward model held out of training** is not: the gap between them opens from 0.8441 at KL 1.0 to **15.5644 at KL 6.0**, and it tracks the true damage closely. That is the detectable signature: **rising KL, rising training reward, and a widening gap to the gold model** — and unlike human evaluation it costs a forward pass.

d.title: A 3,000x cost advantage that is constant in dataset size
d.caption: Both human and AI labelling cost scale linearly with the dataset, so **the advantage never changes relatively** — there is no scale at which AI labelling becomes comparatively better. What changes is the absolute figure crossing a threshold. At a thousand pairs, $3,000 of human labelling is trivially affordable and you should probably just do it: the quality is higher and the cost is noise. At a million pairs, $3,000,000 means **the dataset does not get built at all**. Which reframes RLAIF: it is not a cost optimisation applied to an existing plan, it is what makes a particular size of dataset possible.

nodes.label: Both costs are linear in size
Which is why its quality cost is acceptable

d.title: Constitutional AI replaces the criterion, not just the labeller
d.caption: RLAIF swaps a human labeller for a model and keeps the criterion implicit — whatever the judge model happens to prefer. Constitutional AI additionally replaces the criterion with **something written down**: the model critiques its own output against an explicit set of principles, then revises. Which changes what can be audited. A disagreement about behaviour becomes a disagreement about a **text you can read and edit**, rather than about an annotator pool's tacit preferences.

nodes.label: So disagreements are about the text

d.title: Three kinds of distillation, and the one that surprised everyone
d.caption: Response distillation is what you can do with an **API-only teacher** — generate text, then SFT on it — and it works surprisingly well given how much it throws away. Logit distillation is much richer per token and needs weight access *and* a shared tokeniser, which rules it out across model families. The third row is the result worth knowing: **a 7B SFT'd on reasoning traces beats the same 7B trained with RL directly**, which is 7.9's stage 3 generalised to a different model.

cells.text: needs weights and a shared tokeniser
a 7B so trained beats the same 7B under RL

d.title: What temperature is for, and why the tau-squared factor is there
d.caption: At τ = 1 the teacher puts 0.778 on its top choice and the rest is nearly nothing — so the small differences, which are **where the extra signal lives**, contribute almost no gradient. Raising τ flattens the distribution and amplifies exactly those differences: at τ = 4 the top probability is 0.335 and entropy has nearly doubled. But flattening also shrinks the KL, by **a factor of 13 from τ=1 to τ=4** — which is what the τ² factor compensates, holding the effective gradient magnitude roughly constant so τ can be tuned without retuning the learning rate.

d.title: Why merging more than two models needs TIES
d.caption: The five methods differ mainly in how they handle **interference**, and this measurement is why that matters. Counting parameters where all task vectors agree on sign: **49.9% for two models, 24.9% for three, 6.2% for five** — matching the independent-delta prediction of 2^(1−n) exactly. So a plain average of five fine-tunes is averaging *disagreeing* signs on 94% of parameters, which is how merging produces a model worse than any of its inputs. TIES elects a sign per parameter and averages only the agreeing ones.

d.title: The first branch: is the fact in the weights at all?
d.caption: Scored **as statements**, gpt2 ranks *"The capital of France is Paris"* above the Berlin, Madrid and London variants — so the fact is in the weights. Asked the question directly it gives `' Paris'` **0.54%**. So fine-tuning changes **which continuations are likely, not what is true**: if a fact is absent from the weights, changing the distribution over continuations will not put it there — it will make the model confidently produce something in the right shape. Which is why the answer for facts is retrieval.

nodes.label: Scored as statements: Paris wins
nodes.sub: the fact is in the weights

nodes.label: It produces the right shape, confidently

d.title: The decision tree, keyed on what data you actually have
d.caption: Every row is decided by the **shape of your data** rather than by a quality ranking, which is what makes this usable. The third row is the one people miss: **KTO is the only method that needs no pairs**, so production thumbs-up/thumbs-down is directly usable without constructing comparisons. And the last two rows are where the memory column stops being an aside — 234.7 GB against 117.3 GB is a different class of hardware.

d.title: A reward accuracy of 0.82 is a statement about the loss
d.caption: A doubled RM score and a reward accuracy of 0.82 say something about the objective and nothing about the model. 7.11's simulation makes it concrete: **the training reward rose monotonically through every checkpoint, including the ones where true quality was collapsing.** Someone watching only that number sees a successful run — so the metrics you optimised are the metrics that cannot be used as evidence, and that is a structural property rather than an oversight.

d.title: Six controls, and the two that are not optional
d.caption: The headline is a pairwise win rate against the **pre-alignment** model on held-out prompts. Two controls are mandatory rather than advisable: **randomise order**, because judges favour position A and without it you are measuring position bias plus quality and cannot separate them — and **control for length**, because 7.11 showed length is the canonical hack and 7.6 showed the implicit reward is linear in it. An uncontrolled win rate rewards verbosity and reports it as improvement.
